/politics/2026/oct/12/andy-burnham-brita.headline: How significant are Burnham’s remarks on Kremlin interference in Brexit vote?
/politics/2026/oct/12/andy-burnham-brita.excerpt: Andy Burnham unexpectedly reopened an old Brexit debate when he said he had been told after becoming prime minister that Russia had interfered in the 2016 EU referendum. It was a contentious issue in the second half of the previous decade, but one that had largely been forgotten about as the UK finally adjusted to the reality of leaving the EU. Now Burnham’s comments have given the topic a fresh impetus. What did the prime minister say, and why could it be significant? The Russia topic came up as part of a wide-ranging interview Burnham gave to The Rest is Politics, excerpts of which were released on Sunday, in which he appeared to suggest he had been given new information about the Brexit vote. “I asked the question coming to Downing Street: ‘Was there interference in the 2016 referendum from Russia?’ And I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was,” he said. The prime minister did not say whom he had asked, or set out in detail what the answer was. But his comments suggest he had been given new information of some kind, although he then switched to talking about Russian disinformation in general. “These things are important now to put clearly on the record, and I believe, help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia,” he said. What could Burnham have been told? It was hard to decipher from the interview.
/politics/2026/oct/12/andy-burnham-brita.trail: Prime minister has reopened the debate over whether Russia sought to influence the 2016 referendum

/politics/2026/oct/12/andy-burnham-brita.headline: Burnham: not pursuing better EU deal would be ‘dereliction of duty’
/politics/2026/oct/12/andy-burnham-brita.excerpt: Andy Burnham will put Brexit back on the Commons agenda as MPs return from recess, warning that failing to pursue a better deal with the EU would be a “major dereliction of duty”. The prime minister will use a statement to the Commons on the first day back after the party conference break to urge MPs to face up to the damage caused by Brexit, and embrace closer ties with the EU to increase economic growth and tackle illegal immigration. In a stern warning ahead of the upcoming UK-EU summit, Burnham will argue that Britain cannot afford to turn its back on opportunities for greater cooperation with Europe and that maintaining the status quo is no longer good enough. He will call for a calm, clear-eyed assessment of Britain’s relationship with Europe and urge MPs from across the Commons to back a pragmatic approach. Burnham is expected to argue that most of the public would expect the government to seize the opportunity if closer cooperation could strengthen immigration controls while reviving the economy. A No 10 source said: “Andy understands why some politicians don’t want to face up to the reality that Brexit has not delivered what they once promised. But it is time for a different conversation about what our long-term relationship should be.
/politics/2026/oct/12/andy-burnham-brita.trail: Post-recess statement will focus on damage caused by Brexit and the need to cooperate on immigration and trade

/politics/2026/oct/12/andy-burnham-brita.headline: French minister invites UK to ‘come all the way back’ to the EU
/politics/2026/oct/12/andy-burnham-brita.excerpt: The French finance minister has invited the UK to “come all the way back” to the European Union after Andy Burnham raised the prospect of a new referendum to reverse Brexit. Roland Lescure was speaking after the prime minister used his Labour conference speech to pledge that the government would explore closer ties with the bloc at a summit later this year. He used subsequent interviews to spell out how wide-ranging his consideration of Britain’s future with Brussels could be because Brexit had caused “more harm than good”. Asked about Burnham’s comments, Lescure told the BBC: “British people decided, and that’s obviously their 100% right, and if they’re willing to come back, they will have to decide. But what I can tell them is: come back, anytime.” Lescure said he wanted Britain back in the union to face emerging global threats together. Burnham said last week that the government’s options included keeping the current arrangements in relation to the UK’s relationship with the EU, seeking a customs union, returning to the single market, or going “all the way” with full membership. He said ministers would examine “what is doable” and the “pros and cons” of each option. The prime minister is travelling to Germany for talks with the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, whose government has been supportive of Burnham’s suggestion that the UK could explore closer links with the EU.
/politics/2026/oct/12/andy-burnham-brita.trail: Finance minister, Roland Lescure, welcomes Burnham’s pledge to explore closer ties with bloc

/politics/2026/oct/12/andy-burnham-brita.headline: Could the UK really rejoin the EU?
/politics/2026/oct/12/andy-burnham-brita.excerpt: It was lobbed into the national conversation without fanfare or warning, almost a footnote in the UK prime minister’s first speech as leader to his governing Labour party’s annual conference last week. But Andy Burnham has kicked off a quiet U-turn on Brexit. By stating bluntly that the decision to leave Europe’s core political community had done “more harm than good”, Burnham broke a taboo in his own party, in effect, discarding his predecessor’s paralysing ‘red lines’ on Europe, and signalling he will not be bound by these constraints after the next British election. Over the coming six weeks Burnham will gauge public support before setting out options for the UK’s long term relationship with the UK’s largest market. Rejoining the 27-nation bloc will be one of them. Burnham is opening the door to Britain reversing Brexit. The famous red lines, or non-negotiables, enshrined by Keir Starmer in Labour’s 2024 election manifesto, were meant to reassure Brexit-supporting voters that under Labour there would be no return to a single market, customs union or the free movement of people. But these pledges left Starmer with little room for manoeuvre with Europe, beyond warm words. The evidence that Brexit has stunted the British economy is not new. Estimates for the damage quitting the single market has already done range from 6% of 8% of GDP. What is new is a prime ministerial readiness to publicly acknowledge that harm and conclude that an ambitious new path is required.
/politics/2026/oct/12/andy-burnham-brita.trail: The big question facing ​A​ndy Burnham is not whether Brexit has harmed Britain, but if a rapidly changing Europe will keep the door open​ if the UK decides it wants back in

/politics/2026/oct/12/andy-burnham-brita.headline: Ball in UK’s court: EU ambassador says Brussels will be ‘ready to engage‘ after country decides what it wants
/politics/2026/oct/12/andy-burnham-brita.excerpt: Jukka Salovaara, the newly installed European Union ambassador to the UK, is likely to become a ubiquitous figure in national politics as the Andy Burnham government grapples with the question of its future relationship with the European Union. Burnham has been clearer than his predecessor Keir Starmer in saying that what exists now is not working and that a full range of options, including rejoining, has to be on the table ahead of Labour’s next election manifesto. Salovaara, aged 58, sees his role over the coming years as a “facilitator”, testing both sides like a good diplomat on what might fly and what will not work. He will not sit at the negotiating table, but he will be “very close to it”. “Everyone tells me my job is explaining London to Brussels and Brussels to London”. The UK, he says, remains “the European Union’s first and foremost partner”. When the two have made agreements, it has always been to “our mutual benefit”. A former permanent secretary in Finland’s foreign ministry, who also served as his country’s ambassador to the UN, this is his first job with the European Commission, but not his first posting in the UK. As a young diplomat in the summer of 1996, he handled European affairs in London for Finland at the onset of Cool Britannia, just as Tony Blair was on the cusp of gaining power. “The 1990s was such an optimistic time,” he says of that era. “World trade was growing.
/politics/2026/oct/12/andy-burnham-brita.trail: Jukka Salovaara, who served in London during Cool Britannia era, will be ‘very close’ to negotiations as Burnham government resets relations with EU

/politics/2026/oct/12/nigel-farage-advis.headline: Children and women included in Reform plan to immediately deport 90,000 asylum seekers
/politics/2026/oct/12/nigel-farage-advis.excerpt: Children and mothers would not be exempt from plans by Reform UK to immediately deport 90,000 asylum seekers and impose a five-year ban on people being granted asylum. The party’s most hardline immigration policies to date were condemned by refugee charities and others as “unworkable” and an abandonment of Britain’s tradition of helping victims of war after they were announced by Nigel Farage on Monday. New claims ⁠would be automatically rejected and failed applicants would be returned either to their home countries or a safe third country while a Reform government would impose tariffs, visa bans or airspace restrictions on countries refusing to accept ‌the return of asylum ‌seekers. Asked if children would be exempt, Farage told a press conference in Kent: “If you allow Palestinian or Afghan women to come as well as children, that may well sound compassionate given the circumstances in that country. However, as soon as you do that you open the door to family reunions, to husbands coming, to partners coming, before you know it you have plenty of young men coming as well.” The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said last month that approximately a quarter of arrivals under the reopened UK Resettlement Scheme (UKRS) will consist of Afghan women and girls fleeing Taliban rule and Palestinians who have fled Gaza. A Home Office source said Farage was mistaken in his claim as those coming under the scheme will not have reunion rights.

/politics/2026/oct/12/nigel-farage-advis.headline: Parties prepare for byelection in Farage seat amid speculation over £5m gift inquiry
/politics/2026/oct/12/nigel-farage-advis.excerpt: Nigel Farage’s rivals are gearing up for a byelection in Clacton in the months ahead, amid speculation that the standards inquiry into his £5m gift is nearing a conclusion. Conservative sources said the party was ready to fight in Farage’s seat, although senior figures in the shadow cabinet are divided about whether it would be winnable, given Farage’s victory in a byelection over the summer. Other parties, including the hard-right Restore Britain, are also expected to put up candidates in the seat this time, after boycotting the August poll. Westminster is poised for a battle over the future of Reform if the sanction from the standards inquiry is a heavy one. The process could theoretically take place before Christmas if a decision is imminent, but the timelines of previous cases suggest it is more likely to be next year – if a serious sanction is imposed. In the cases of Margaret Ferrier, the SNP MP who broke lockdown rules, and Peter Bone, the Tory MP found to have bullied staff, it took well over six months from the conclusion of the commissioner’s report for a byelection to take place. The investigation into Farage’s gift began after the Guardian revealed in May that the crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne had given him £5m just before the last election in 2024. The Reform leader has said it was a personal matter, not political, and the money did not need to be declared.
/politics/2026/oct/12/nigel-farage-advis.trail: Tories said to be ready to fight in Clacton, with standards investigation rumoured to be nearing its end

/politics/2026/oct/12/nigel-farage-advis.headline: Bragging rights for Burnham, blues for Farage: conference season winners and losers
/politics/2026/oct/12/nigel-farage-advis.excerpt: Winners Andy Burnham Even his fiercest critics would struggle to argue that Andy Burnham’s first conference as Labour party leader was anything but a success. There was the requisite rapture among the Labour faithful after his deeply-personal speech, delivered without a tie or a lectern and, at times, with tears in his eyes. But even figures on the right, such as the broadcaster Piers Morgan, described it as “one of the best, and most powerfully delivered, by a British politician in a very long time”. The prime minister’s policy offering packed a punch too. He put forward radical progressive policies on social care, promising to “rip the plaster off” and make changes to the pensions triple lock, electoral reform and Europe. A YouGov poll after the conference showed that it had boosted the “Burnham bounce”, with Labour opening up a five-point lead over Reform UK in the polls. The upcoming budget, and next year’s spending review, will sorely test whether he can keep that momentum going and make good on his promises. Burnham’s success at the Labour conference was capped by a victory at the Holborn and St Pancras byelection a few days later seeing off a challenge by the leader of the Green party Zack Polanski. Kemi Badenoch This time last year, Kemi Badenoch was hanging on to her role as leader of the opposition by a thread. But in the past 12 months her personal favourability ratings have continued to improve, according to More in Common research.
/politics/2026/oct/12/nigel-farage-advis.trail: While the Labour and Conservative leaders will be delighted with their showing, Nigel Farage, Ed Davey and Zack Polanski have less reason for cheer

/politics/2026/oct/12/nigel-farage-advis.headline: Reform clears its own officials of breaking party funding laws despite police investigation
/politics/2026/oct/12/nigel-farage-advis.excerpt: Reform UK has cleared two of its senior officials of breaking laws that ban foreign donations, despite the matter remaining under police investigation. The party published a 27-page report of an internal inquiry finding that Dan Jukes, Nigel Farage’s press adviser, and James Orr, its head of policy, had not breached funding rules. Party sources said they intended to pursue legal action against the undercover reporting group Verbatim, whose footage led to the investigation and was broadcast by Channel 4 News. However, Labour said the report was a “whitewash” given it was undertaken by the party’s legal secretary, Adam Richardson, a barrister with a longstanding association with the party, and Tom Waterhouse, its general secretary. Labour also said it was not credible for the party to distance itself from the scandal by claiming Orr and Jukes, two of Farage’s top team, were just contractors. Police have been investigating potential offences under electoral law since the broadcast in early September, saying they would widen an existing special inquiry relating to donations made to Reform. Jukes, 30, and Orr, 47, will remain suspended by the party while the police inquiry continues. Jukes and Orr were filmed talking about a scheme in which a US donor paid for three polls with favourable narratives for Reform, costing more than £30,000. Donations from overseas sources are not allowed under political funding laws.
/politics/2026/oct/12/nigel-farage-advis.trail: Internal inquiry exonerates Dan Jukes and James Orr, who were filmed talking about scheme involving US donor

/politics/2026/oct/12/nigel-farage-advis.headline: Nigel Farage questioned by standards commissioner over £5m gift
/politics/2026/oct/12/nigel-farage-advis.excerpt: Nigel Farage has been interviewed by the standards commissioner for an investigation into whether he should have declared a £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne. The Reform UK leader spent about half an hour being questioned over the money, the Sunday Times reported. Farage maintains the gift was for his personal security. The interview conducted last month is a sign the process is nearing a conclusion, although Reform UK is not believed to have been informed that the report is finished. An MP under investigation is usually notified before the conclusion of the process. If the commissioner finds that there has been a serious breach of the rules, the matter is passed to the standards committee of MPs and lay members, which can ask for further evidence. The committee can recommend a sanction or override the report. If it suggests more than a 10-day suspension from the Commons – and parliament agrees – the Reform UK leader could find himself facing a recall petition and second byelection in his Clacton constituency. Farage has been under investigation over the gift since shortly after the Guardian revealed in May that Harborne had given him £5m just before the last election in 2024. The Reform leader has said it was a personal matter, not political, and the money did not need to be declared. The rules state that financial support related to an MP’s job needs to be registered if given in the 12 months before they enter parliament.
/politics/2026/oct/12/nigel-farage-advis.trail: Reform UK leader was interviewed for half an hour last month over money from crypto billionaire

/business/2026/oct/13/ai-share-crash-ris.headline: France’s dilemma: protesters demand spending as markets require fiscal restraint
/business/2026/oct/13/ai-share-crash-ris.excerpt: Eight years have passed since rising fuel prices brought the gilets jaunes (yellow vest) demonstrators to the streets of France, prompting the first big crisis of Emmanuel Macron’s time in the Élysée Palace. As the French president contemplates his exit next year, turmoil has again gripped the streets in the form of student protests, but this time the financial markets are unhappy too. Investors are concerned about the government’s failure to bring spending under control and end a long period of “fiscal incontinence”. Financial markets are unnerved by similar trends in the UK, the US and more recently Italy, causing jitters in global bond markets. But it’s France that has become the biggest worry, hemmed in by debts across the public and private sectors, limiting their scope to dig the country out of a deepening hole. France’s debt-to-GDP stood at 115.6% in 2025, while its budget deficit was 5.1%, compared with 94.3% and 4.3% for the UK respectively. In Britain, the chancellor, John Healey, is on course to reduce the budget deficit this year and in 2027. His French counterpart, Roland Lescure, has promised to follow suit after a rise to 5.4% this year, but has yet to say how. ‘I am panicking’ One victim of the uncertainty is business investment. A survey by Medef, France’s largest employer federation, showed 82% of firms were pessimistic about the impact of the next government’s economic policy.
/business/2026/oct/13/ai-share-crash-ris.trail: Waves of protests expose debt crisis faced by French government, but political wrangling is stalling an escape plan. Is there a way out?

/business/2026/oct/13/ai-share-crash-ris.headline: Oil price rise creates more pressure on UK policymakers before budget
/business/2026/oct/13/ai-share-crash-ris.excerpt: Oil prices lurched upwards again on Thursday, creating a growing headache for UK policymakers ahead of John Healey’s budget next month. While Healey has been keen to present an upbeat picture of the UK’s economic prospects, Treasury sources concede the sharp jump in oil and gas prices means they have “less room” than a month ago. Officials are working “at pace” on a range of possible options for supporting consumers, particularly if high prices persist, feeding through into a sharp rise in the quarterly energy price cap in January. But any package is expected to fall far short of the costly across-the-board subsidies announced by Liz Truss in 2022, with the Treasury mindful of the measures already taken, including Andy Burnham’s VAT cut on electricity bills. Options are believed to include shifting more green subsidies into general taxation, echoing the approach taken by Rachel Reeves, or targeting help at the poorest households – though some officials are sceptical about how effectively this can be achieved. The price of a barrel of Brent crude was up almost 5% at $108 on Thursday after reports of more military clashes between Saudi Arabia and Houthi forces. Donald Trump has given little indication of how, or when, the wider US-Israeli war on Iran could be brought to a close, despite the impact on gasoline prices in the US before crucial midterm elections.
/business/2026/oct/13/ai-share-crash-ris.trail: Treasury sources concede ‘less room’ for manoeuvre as global bond selloff also hikes government’s borrowing costs

/business/2026/oct/13/ai-share-crash-ris.headline: Surging inflation puts interest rates back in focus as policymakers meet in Japan, US and UK
/business/2026/oct/13/ai-share-crash-ris.excerpt: Central bankers in economies including the US, Japan and the UK will face a moment of truth this week, as surging inflation raises the prospect of higher interest rates. Policymakers in all three countries will set rates in the next seven days against the backdrop of turbulent global bond markets. In particular, investors will be watching closely to see if Kevin Warsh, the new chair of the US Federal Reserve, can face down Donald Trump’s demands for rate cuts and instead persuade Fed governors to raise them on Wednesday. Warsh was handpicked by the US president, who has repeatedly demanded lower interest rates. In a Truth Social post this month, Trump claimed the US should have the “LOWEST RATE of any country in the World”. He added: “The Fed Board, with its great new leader, must get smart – BE PATRIOTS for a change.” However, the central bank’s board of governors is having to contend with a renewed rise in oil prices after the US-Iran conflict intensified again. The cost of a barrel of crude surged past $100 last week for the first time since July, as the strait of Hormuz remained all but closed to tanker traffic and Houthi rebels advanced along the Red Sea coast, threatening to choke off Saudi oil supplies. Oil prices eased slightly on Friday amid hopes of fresh talks to reopen the waterway but remained well above levels in the summer, when Middle East hostilities temporarily abated.
/business/2026/oct/13/ai-share-crash-ris.trail: Iran war and turbulent global bond markets add to pressure as rate decisions loom this week in major western economies

/business/2026/oct/13/ai-share-crash-ris.headline: China prepares £40bn stimulus for financial sector amid fears over sluggish growth
/business/2026/oct/13/ai-share-crash-ris.excerpt: China will inject $54bn (£40bn) into its financial sector as Beijing attempts to shore up banks and insurers in the face of faltering economic growth. A host of financial institutions said they were due to receive billions of yuan in capital from state institutions including the ministry of finance and even the company that runs the country’s tobacco monopoly. The stimulus is designed to help China bolster the ability of its financial sector to invest in the stock market and lend to businesses, amid signs that the world’s second largest economy is struggling to escape weak growth. The country’s largest life insurer, China Life Insurance, will get 35bn yuan, while the China Taiping Insurance Group said it would receive 7bn. The People’s Insurance ⁠Company of China said it planned to raise up to 15bn yuan through a private placement of A-shares – stock that specifically allows investors to trade in China-based companies – to the ministry of finance, with the proceeds used to replenish ‌its capital. The initiative could help bolster ‌state insurers that have been directed by Beijing to support the stock market with medium- and long-term funds, while positioning them to help regulators ‌manage smaller, higher-risk insurance companies. The insurance sector has been struggling with eroding profitability owing to persistently low interest rates, with numerous small and mid-sized insurers reporting deteriorating solvency ratios, a measure of financial health.
/business/2026/oct/13/ai-share-crash-ris.trail: Beijing wants banks and insurers to bolster investment in stock market as it helps to replenish cash reserves

/business/2026/oct/13/ai-share-crash-ris.headline: Global bond sell-off intensifies as US-Iran tensions stoke inflation fears
/business/2026/oct/13/ai-share-crash-ris.excerpt: The global government bond sell-off resumed on Wednesday, driving up the UK’s borrowing costs and exacerbating the challenges facing John Healey as he prepares his first budget. The yield – effectively the interest rate – on 10-year UK government bonds, or gilts, jumped to just below 5.3% in early trading: its highest level since mid-2008. Investors across major markets have been dumping bonds in recent days amid fears about inflation and spiralling deficits. Global inflation fears have intensified since the US and Iran began exchanging fire again at the weekend, pushing up the oil price and increasing expectations that central banks will have to raise interest rates in the coming months. Higher bond yields progressively increase the cost of financing the government’s debt. UK analysts have warned that higher gilt yields since the start of the Iran war have potentially wiped out almost half of Healey’s headroom against the government’s fiscal rules. Economists at Deutsche Bank reckon the £26bn room for manoeuvre Rachel Reeves created at her spring forecast could be down to less than £14bn by the time of the 28 October budget. Healey would then have to decide whether to rebuild the margin for error with tax increases or spending cuts – alongside facing pressure to fund higher defence spending.
/business/2026/oct/13/ai-share-crash-ris.trail: UK borrowing costs driven up, adding to challenges facing John Healey as he prepares for first budget

/education/2026/oct/13/english-councils-.headline: Labour Send changes at risk as parents rush to secure support, say experts
/education/2026/oct/13/english-councils-.excerpt: Labour’s flagship changes to special education in England are at risk of unravelling because parents are rushing to secure support for their children before the system changes, new analysis has found. The Institute for Government (IfG) thinktank says the government’s plans to largely replace education, health and care plans (EHCPs) in England with more widespread support in mainstream schools may be too optimistic and take longer to complete than its 2030 timeline. The thinktank’s report calls on the government to review the timetable for the changes. And it suggests that if ministers do not act they “risk basing both their reforms and spending plans on assumptions that the system cannot deliver”. The news will be seen as a sign that the government’s ambitious plans to overhaul the special education system did not reckon with the scale of worry among parents, many of whom appear to have acted to ensure support and avoid uncertainty in the future. The Guardian recently reported that councils and schools have reported a surge in applications for EHCPs, with one school describing the level as “unreal” compared with previous years. Several councils are now projecting that at the current rates of increase, nearly one in 10 pupils will have an EHCP by 2029. Amber Dellar, the author of the IfG report out this week, said the long rollout of the changes created a “moral hazard” that encouraged parents to apply for EHCPs now rather than wait for the new system.
/education/2026/oct/13/english-councils-.trail: Overhaul of special education in England could unravel, thinktank finds, because of ‘use it before you lose it’ dynamic

/education/2026/oct/13/english-councils-.headline: Pupils with Send plans in England likely to double to one in 10 in rush for support
/education/2026/oct/13/english-councils-.excerpt: Schools and councils across England are expecting the proportion of children with special needs plans to double to one in 10, with families rushing to secure support before ministers bring in changes. Headteachers have reported an “unreal” surge in applications for education, health and care plans (EHCPs) mandating support for needs or disabilities such as speech and learning difficulties, autism or ADHD. In 2025, just one in 20 school-age children had EHCPs. The number of pupils with EHCPs has risen by more than 11% in each of the past two years, and projections by local authorities seen by the Guardian are anticipating similar double-digit annual increases over the next three years. Similar levels nationally would mean just under 10% of all school-age children with an EHCP in 2029. Such a rapid increase would outstrip the government’s own forecasts and eat into funding for improving specialist support in mainstream schools, undermining its plans for immediate reform while straining school and council budgets. School leaders said their special educational needs (Send) coordinators had worked through the summer to deal with the influx of requests for assessments, as secondary schools say that many more year 7 pupils are arriving with EHCPs or applications. One described the volume of requests as “unreal”, while other schools said they expected to have double the number of incoming pupils with EHCPs when the new academic year begins this month.
/education/2026/oct/13/english-councils-.trail: Schools and councils express financial concerns as EHCP applications surge before potential change in provision

/education/2026/oct/13/english-councils-.headline: ‘Powerful example’: minister looks to Essex school for blueprint to transform Send provision
/education/2026/oct/13/english-councils-.excerpt: Georgia Gould is in a race against time. And the minister responsible for overhauling England’s special educational needs provision is hoping that a state school in Colchester will help her beat the clock. Gould visited Thomas Lord Audley secondary school last week to see the secrets of its success in persuading local parents that it can help children with special needs thrive in a mainstream setting. Under the government’s proprosals announced in February, more funding and universal support are to be given to mainstream schools to accommodate children and young people with special educational needs and disabilities (Send). The schools minister told the Guardian that institutions such as Thomas Lord Audley are doing many things that will become national policy under the new system. “What they are doing here is a really powerful example of best practice,” Gould said, explaining how the school engages with families and pupils a year or more in advance of entry, and draws up bespoke plans for pupils’ needs similar to the government’s proposed digital records to track and share day-to-day support for children with special needs, called individual support plans. Gould said: “Part of the work we are trying to do, to transform the system towards inclusion, is to take the best practices from schools like this, and make sure that people can see the evidence and the impact they have on things like attendance … And then we want to spread that practice.
/education/2026/oct/13/english-councils-.trail: Georgia Gould says moving system towards inclusion will mean parents ‘don’t need to fight’ for support in future

/society/2026/oct/13/women-autoimmune-co.headline: US maternity wards face wave of closures as Medicaid cuts kick in
/society/2026/oct/13/women-autoimmune-co.excerpt: Maternity wards across the United States are facing a wave of closures as cuts to federal Medicaid funding take effect, experts have warned. According to analysis by the non-profit Protect Our Care, 52 maternity wards have closed since the HR1 bill was announced in July 2025, with a further eight having announced their upcoming closure. The bill, which will fully come into effect in the new year, will result in many adults covered through Medicaid having to meet new work requirements and being subject to more frequent eligibility checks, while there will be less federal funding for states for Medicaid. Hospitals which have already permanently closed their maternity wards include the Centra Southside Community hospital in Virginia and St Mary’s Sacred Heart hospital in rural north-east Georgia, which both cited upcoming federal policy changes to Medicaid as a reason. Experts are expecting to see more closures of maternity units in the run-up to and after the federal changes to Medicaid come into effect in the new year. “We’re deeply concerned that these changes already have and will continue to worsen an already serious maternity care crisis,” said Erin Jones, senior director of legislative and strategic counsel of the non-profit March of Dimes.
/society/2026/oct/13/women-autoimmune-co.trail: Trump’s ‘big, beautiful bill’ spending cuts will be fully felt next year, but hospitals are already feeling the squeeze

/society/2026/oct/13/women-autoimmune-co.headline: Women suffer more pain than men across the whole body, major global study finds
/society/2026/oct/13/women-autoimmune-co.excerpt: Women report suffering more pain than men, a major new global study has found. That was true for all types of pain the researchers measured, and comes amid continuing concern about the gender pain gap, which means women are less likely to be prescribed the pain relief they need. Researchers from all over the world carried out “one of the largest harmonisation efforts in pain epidemiology to date”. Data was collected from more than 6 million people from 118 countries from 1990 to 2025, and included people from aged five years to more than 100. The research, published in Nature Medicine, looked at how pain, as the leading global cause of disability, was distributed both around the world and across the human lifespan. It found women’s self-reported pain across 11 bodily sites – head, face, neck or shoulder, foot or ankle, hand or wrist, elbow, chest, back, stomach or abdomen, hip and knee – was higher than for men. That was particularly true for headache, facial and abdominal pain. For men and women, the steepest increase in pain happened before people turned 55, then peaked at or beyond 75, with back, hip and knee pain increasing across the lifespan. That indicated “that a substantial share of lifetime pain burden develops during working-age adulthood”, the authors wrote. About 40% of participants reported back pain, while facial pain was the rarest at 2%.

/society/2026/oct/13/women-autoimmune-co.headline: Tell us: what happened after you froze your eggs?
/society/2026/oct/13/women-autoimmune-co.excerpt: Oocyte cryopreservation, more commonly known as egg freezing, has been around for decades but the procedure stopped being considered experimental in 2012. Since then, elective egg freezing has boomed. Often represented as an insurance policy against age- or illness-related fertility decline, the process can be costly and complex. While figures vary, research suggests most people who undergo egg freezing never access their eggs and results are mixed for those who do. Long-term storage poses its own costs and questions. We want to hear from people who froze their eggs five, 10 or even 15 years ago about what happened next. Did the “insurance” buy you peace of mind? /society/2026/oct/13/women-autoimmune-co.headline: Menopause supplements costing more than £400 a year ‘no better than cheap multivitamin’
/society/2026/oct/13/women-autoimmune-co.excerpt: Menopause supplements costing more than £400 a year are no better than a £22-a-year multivitamin, according to analysis by the consumer watchdog Which?. Which? found that many popular supplements that are aimed at women over 45 going through menopause or perimenopause lack meaningful quantities of key nutrients, yet cost 20 times more than standard multivitamins. The global menopause supplement market is valued at nearly $17bn and is expected to reach $25bn by 2030, as women look for ways to manage a variety of symptoms associated with menopause such as hot flushes, poor sleep and mood swings. But research by Which? found that none of the supplements it studied contained the correct nutrients in the right doses to support their use for menopause. Shefalee Loth, a public health nutritionist at Which? who co-led the research, said: “Which? is concerned that the supplements industry has become a wild west and regulators are not doing enough to get a grip on dubious marketing and unchecked quasi-medical claims from firms apparently seeking to cash in on people’s health anxiety and insecurities.” Calcium and vitamin D are the most important nutrients during perimenopause and menopause as they support bone health as oestrogen levels decline. Maintaining good levels of iron, magnesium and other vitamins and minerals can also help with symptoms. Nutritionists from Which?
/society/2026/oct/13/women-autoimmune-co.trail: Many products aimed at women over 45 lack meaningful quantities of key nutrients, consumer watchdog Which? found

/society/2026/oct/13/women-autoimmune-co.headline: UK doctors develop non-invasive test for womb cancer in women bleeding after menopause
/society/2026/oct/13/women-autoimmune-co.excerpt: Doctors have developed a simple test that could help rule out womb cancer in women who experience bleeding after menopause. The approach has the potential to transform care for thousands of women each year and spare them from invasive and uncomfortable tests that can also be costly for healthcare systems. Every year, hundreds of thousands of women worldwide are diagnosed with womb cancer. Bleeding after menopause triggers an urgent cancer referral but only about 5% to 10% of women who report bleeding have an underlying cancer. Currently, the tests for womb cancer – an internal ultrasound scan, a biopsy of the womb lining and hysteroscopy, in which a camera is passed into the womb – are all invasive and costly. The new test, developed at the University of Manchester and Manchester University NHS foundation trust, looks at cells collected from the urine and vaginal fluid. It is cheap and non-invasive. In a study assessing the test, 1,864 women attending seven hospitals in north-west England with postmenopausal bleeding gave a urine sample and a vaginal fluid sample before their routine tests. Of these women, 5% (99 of the 1,864) were diagnosed with womb cancer via a biopsy or surgery. Using the new test, cytologists unaware of the women’s diagnoses identified 80 of the 99 womb cancers and correctly returned a negative result for 93% of women who did not have womb cancer. The findings were published in the journal Lancet Obstetrics, Gynaecology, & Women’s Health.
/society/2026/oct/13/women-autoimmune-co.trail: Test using urine and vaginal fluid samples raises hopes thousands of lower-risk women could be spared internal ultrasounds and hysteroscopies

/food/2026/oct/13/whale-meat-curry-1920s.headline: ‘Pungent and mealy’: the best (and worst) supermarket tuna, tasted and rated
/food/2026/oct/13/whale-meat-curry-1920s.excerpt: Eaten straight from the tin, without seasoning, lemon, olive oil or mayonnaise, canned tuna is pretty gruelling stuff, not least because it’s pungent, mealy and hard to swallow. Testing tuna in this way demonstrates the overall poor quality of the product and why certain brands and species are revered for their superior texture and flavour. That said, a tuna mayo sandwich is one of my go-to lunches, so long as the fish is sustainably sourced (so as not to leave a bad taste in the mouth) and there’s enough pepper to balance out its flavour. Skipjack is a fast-growing species with a softer, flakier texture and fishier flavour than some others. Albacore tuna, meanwhile, is a larger, slower-growing fish, which makes it more sensitive to overfishing. Its flesh is much paler and more delicately flavoured, with large, meaty flakes. The Marine Conservation Society (MCS) is an independent registered environmental charity that uses scientific evidence to rate the sustainability of seafood. Its Good Fish Guide uses a traffic-light system from green (best choice) to red (fish to avoid). Both skipjack and albacore have green-rated options available. However, fish sustainability is complicated and depends on the catch method, region and species. The Good Fish Guide rates pole and line as the best catch method, and recommends fish certified by the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC).

/food/2026/oct/13/whale-meat-curry-1920s.headline: Why we’re all hooked on tinned fish
/food/2026/oct/13/whale-meat-curry-1920s.excerpt: I can’t find it, despite having spent the past 35 minutes looking, but somewhere in the house is The Crisis Cook Book. It’s a standard paperback, postbox-red with white writing on the cover, and full of recipes from chefs including Rowley Leigh, Heston Blumenthal and Jeremy Lee. Not having found it, I needed Amazon to tell me it was published in 2007 and compiled by Nick Lander, at the time the Financial Times’ restaurant correspondent. He asked 28 chefs to donate three recipes – their favourite starter, main course and dessert – and proceeds from the book went to the national homelessness charity Crisis. The reason I needed (and still need – it is now a mission) to find the book is because inside it is Rowley’s recipe for pasta with tinned sardines, fennel, chilli and lemon zest. It’s a recipe that I have made so many times, and for so many years, that I don’t need to look at the book; but, equally, because I’ve made it so many times and so much time has passed, I have no idea how far I have drifted from the original, and want to check. I’ve even written about this recipe in my weekly Guardian column, without referring to the book or even mentioning Rowley! Not that a store-cupboard version of the Sicilian pasta con le sarde (pasta with sardines and wild fennel) is owned by anyone, although Rowley did teach me.
/food/2026/oct/13/whale-meat-curry-1920s.trail: Sardines, mackerel, herring, pilchards, sprats and anchovies ... canning only makes the umami flavour better. They’re my top choice for pasta

/food/2026/oct/13/whale-meat-curry-1920s.headline: ​My coastal road trip confirms that seaside ​food ​still ​beats ​fine ​dining
/food/2026/oct/13/whale-meat-curry-1920s.excerpt: There are few things more powerful than the smell of salt, vinegar and hot oil carried on a sea breeze. Or sugar-coated doughnuts, still warm in a grease-stained paper bag. Such distinctly British perfumes are the smell of my summer, because my family and I are road-tripping through the UK and Ireland. We are embracing as much of coastline as we can, while battling seagulls and unpredictable weather along the way. And, unlike the carefully curated dining experiences we seek on holidays abroad, seaside food has always been wonderfully simple. It is rarely elegant, but it is pure comfort and nostalgia. First up, fish and chips, in my opinion, they remain the undisputed king of Britain’s coastal cuisine. Every seaside town insists that theirs is the best (so far, the finest I’ve tried were in Yorkshire, but I am prepared for that to change on this holiday). If you are at home this summer, or not near a British seaside, you can, of course, have a go at making your own. Tim Hughes’s and Felicity Cloake’s recipes are as authentic as they come, along with a crisp beer batter for firm white fish. For a slight twist, Yotam Ottolenghi’s fish and spiced sweet potato chips is an excellent, inspired dish. Either way, all options deliver. Next on my list of seaside classics is a paper bag of hot doughnuts and a 99 Flake ice-cream.
/food/2026/oct/13/whale-meat-curry-1920s.trail: ​A​ family holiday shaped by salt air, seagulls and unpredictable weather proves that the seaside serves a kind of joy no restaurant can engineer

/food/2026/oct/13/whale-meat-curry-1920s.headline: ‘Why did it become personal?’: furore over plans to expand Kent oyster shack
/food/2026/oct/13/whale-meat-curry-1920s.excerpt: The clink of glasses and the lapping of the tide was punctuated by giggling toddlers and the slurp of oysters at tables populated by people gently sizzling on a baking day on the Kent seaside. But James Green, of the Whitstable Oyster Fishery Company, had the demeanour of a man who had found grit in his mollusc. “I don’t like to use the term but it is nimbyism,” he said. “Why did it become personal? I don’t know really. Because we’re a family business, it’s a relatively small town?” Green, 58, is the director of the WOFC, a company he inherited from his father and whose roots can be traced back to 1793. He has become embroiled in a battle over his plans for a seafood empire. The WOFC harvests about 2m oysters a year from Whitstable’s seabeds, half of which stay on the north Kent coast to be sold in the company’s hotel and the four restaurants it runs on the front. It is Green’s application to extend the seating of one of those restaurants, the Forge oyster shack, on to a patch of beach used to store boats belonging to members of the Whitstable Yacht Club, that has caused a furore and which he says highlights a national problem. Green is battling, he says, to grow a business that employs 200 people but could take on more, and which has cemented Whitstable’s reputation as “Britain’s Oysteropolis”. The new seating for the Forge would allow visitors to enjoy “half a dozen oysters and a glass of muscadet” on the sand, he said, and offer further reason to visit the town.
/food/2026/oct/13/whale-meat-curry-1920s.trail: James Green’s oyster company owns a chunk of Whitstable’s shoreline but success has not brought affection from residents

/food/2026/oct/13/whale-meat-curry-1920s.headline: ‘Intense, salty, foul’: the best (and worst) supermarket anchovies, tasted and rated
/food/2026/oct/13/whale-meat-curry-1920s.excerpt: To taste these anchovies, I invited a friend, the food journalist and author Sudi Pigott, to join me. Arriving with a packet of Pujadó Solano anchovies and her new book, Consider the Anchovy, in hand, she and I tasted 10 brands of anchovies straight from the tin or jar with sparkling water and cucumber to cleanse the palate. According to Pigott, the best anchovies are “juicy, plump and velvety, with a sweet, nutty taste of jamón!” The anchovy supply chain has been heavily affected by El Niño, which caused abnormal weather events in Peru, where the most economical anchovies in our test were fished, and a shortage severe enough to threaten global supply and push up prices. Premium anchovies sourced from the Bay of Biscay (the Cantabrian Sea) have seen prices rise, too, driven more by growing international demand than any shortage, because the stock itself remains healthy. We scored anchovies on appearance, texture (including pin bones), flavour and value. I was shocked at the variation in quality in this category from minnow-sized, stubbly and tough brown fillets that were unbelievably salty to the most remarkably flavoured, tender, rose-coloured fillets that reminded us of serrano ham. *** The best supermarket anchovies *** Best overall: Waitrose No 1 Cantabrian anchovy fillets in extra-virgin olive oil £1.75 for 50g at Waitrose (£3.50/100g) ★★★★☆ Small, dusky-pink fillets. Seductively sweet, smooth and salty but well balanced in flavour.
/food/2026/oct/13/whale-meat-curry-1920s.trail: We put 10 tinned and jarred varieties to the test to see which anchovies are the best catch for your cash
